title: Which job needs an agent?
scenario: Your studio has three requests on the board. You decide which ones get an agent, a fixed workflow, or one call. Use the exhibit. The job list and the log are our own examples, made up for this case.
exhibit:
Three requests on the board (job names are ours):
  Job A  Every Monday, take the approved hero ad and export it as 9:16, 1:1
         and 16:9. Same three sizes, same folder, every week.
  Job B  A new snack brand has a vague brief: "fresh, loud, not like the
         others". Find three creative directions, test ideas, drop the weak
         ones, and bring back the best.
  Job C  One image of a mug on a wooden table for a menu. One prompt is
         ready and approved.

Agent loop log for an earlier job like B (made up for this case)
  model call 1 -> asks for make_image  (tool runs)
  model call 2 -> asks for make_image  (tool runs)
  model call 3 -> asks for make_image  (tool runs)
  model call 4 -> asks for check_file  (tool runs)
  ...
  model call 14 -> final answer

questions.prompt: Which job fits an agent best?

options.text: Job A, because it repeats every Monday and an agent never gets bored of repeating work
options.explanation: Repeating is a sign of fixed steps, which fit a workflow. Anthropic says to add complexity only when it is needed.

options.text: Job B, because nobody can list the steps in advance and the model must try and choose
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic says agents suit open-ended problems where you cannot predict the number of steps or hardcode a path.

options.text: Job C, because a single image is the most important thing the studio makes this week
options.explanation: How important the image is does not change the need. One approved prompt needs one call, not a loop.

options.text: All three jobs, because an agent can do any job and so it is the safer choice for everything
options.explanation: Anthropic recommends the simplest solution that works, and says that can mean not building an agentic system.

questions.prompt: What fits Job A, the Monday export of three sizes?

options.text: An agent that picks the sizes it thinks are best each week, using its own judgment
options.explanation: The sizes never change, so there is nothing for the model to judge. Free choice only adds risk.

options.text: Three separate chats, with a person typing the same request by hand each Monday morning
options.explanation: This works, but it adds hand work to a job whose steps are already known. A fixed workflow removes that work.

options.text: A workflow with fixed steps: the same three exports, in the same order, each Monday
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic defines a workflow as models and tools orchestrated through predefined code paths. Fixed steps make cost and result easy to predict.

options.text: A managed agent that runs for hours, so it can find new sizes the client might also like
options.explanation: A long run adds cost and unknown results. The client asked for three sizes, and nothing more.

questions.prompt: What fits Job C, the mug image with one approved prompt?

options.text: An agent with five tools, so that the model can review and improve the prompt on its own
options.explanation: The prompt is already approved. An agent would add trips round the loop for no gain.

options.text: A team of specialist agents, one to write, one to draw and one to judge the picture
options.explanation: More agents mean more prompts, cost and review. It is far too much for one image.

options.text: A workflow with three review steps, which is the safest option for a menu picture
options.explanation: Review steps add work. For one approved prompt the lowest step on the ladder is enough.

options.text: One call to an image model with the approved prompt, then a person looks at the result
options.explanation: Right. Anthropic says that for many applications a single model call is enough. Start there, and move up only when it fails.

questions.prompt: The log for a Job B-style run shows 14 model calls. What does this tell you for planning?

options.text: The count was set by the model, so the cost cannot be known in advance and limits must be planned first
options.explanation: Right. In an agent loop the model decides how many trips to take. Anthropic notes higher costs for agents, and Google says one managed-agent interaction typically uses 100k to 3M tokens.

options.text: Fourteen is the normal number for every agent run, so you can budget for exactly fourteen
options.explanation: Nothing sets a normal count. The same kind of job can take far fewer or far more trips.

options.text: The calls cost nothing, because only the image tool itself is billed to the studio account
options.explanation: Each model call uses tokens. Google's page counts token use for agent loops.

options.text: The extra calls show a bug, because a correct agent would have finished in a single trip
options.explanation: A loop with many trips is how agents work. It is not by itself a bug, but it is why cost is hard to predict.
